item.title: Correlated Quantal Response Equilibrium: A New Equilibrium Notion for Human-AI Strategic Interactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.29020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The modeling of the behavior of agents in strategic environments and the prediction of the resulting outcomes has long been a challenging problem; this has been the focus of game theory. The introduction of AI agents as human-aids or as sole decision-makers expands the underlying question: Can we model behavior and predict outcomes of strategic games that involve a mix of AI agents and human players? As an initial answer, we propose Correlated Quantal Response Equilibrium (CQRE) that combines and generalizes classical solution concepts such as Quantal Response Equilibrium and Correlated Equilibrium. We answer questions of existence and propose a method for computing the CQRE that is a best fit to a given joint action distribution. We demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of CQRE predictions using a diverse collection of complex general-sum games, including high-rank and large-action two-player games, challenging multiplayer games, and a large-scale extension of the Selten--Chmura setting to AI--AI and human--AI play.
item.dc:creator: Zehao Zhao, Rahul Jain, Vijay Subramanian

item.title: Cycle structure of best-response dynamics in random bimatrix games
item.description: arXiv:2610.29153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the best-response dynamics in games with random payoffs. We consider two-player bimatrix games, with $n$ strategies each. We assume that payoffs come from a continuous distribution, and study the best-response dynamics of these games, after imposing some structure on their payoff matrices. In particular, we focus on symmetric games, antisymmetric games, common-interest games, zero-sum games, and games with independent payoffs. When two players take turns in playing the best response to the opponent's action, they eventually end up cycling through the same sequence of actions. The main focus of the paper is the cycle structure of large random games. In particular, we study the number of cycles, the number of cycles of a certain length, the length of the longest cycle, and related quantities. We show that the structure of the game has an important impact on the typical cycle structure. Our arguments are based on a representation of the best-response dynamics of these games as directed bipartite graphs, and on the cycle structure that arises in them.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Nikolaos Karelas, G\'abor Lugosi, Rui-Ray Zhang

item.title: Pareto Inefficiency of EFX
item.description: arXiv:2610.29201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of allocating indivisible goods to agents with additive valuations, under two classic notions of fairness and efficiency: envy-freeness up to any good (EFX) and Pareto optimality. While some of the earliest work on EFX showed that Pareto optimal EFX allocations may not exist if agents can have zero value for some goods, it has remained open whether the same is true when all values are positive. We present a simple instance in which every good has positive value to every agent, but no Pareto optimal EFX allocation exists. We then generalize to a family of instances showing that Pareto optimal $\alpha$-EFX allocations may not exist for any $\alpha > 2/3$.
item.dc:creator: Sepideh Mahabadi, Prasanna Ramakrishnan, Jakub Tarnawski

item.title: When Are We Near Nash? Certifying Solutions in General-Sum Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.29300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heuristic solvers for general-sum extensive-form games produce a stream of iterates, and practice reports the NashGap of the returned profile. We ask what a solver can know about its own iterates from the regret accumulators and the terminal-distribution accumulators its updates already maintain. In two-player games the NashGap of a weighted average strategy equals, at the maximizing player, the weighted external regret plus a signed value correction. Bounding the regret by the running counterfactual-regret accumulator gives an online certificate whose cost per checkpoint is linear in the number of terminal histories. The certificate stays sound under alternating updates and in games with three or more players. The mismatch between what alternation evaluates and what the averages record enters as one signed comparator term, maximized in a single backward pass per player whose comparator weight is nonzero. The bound is read off the regret state, with no best response against the average. Run a portfolio of training-free regret-matching solvers, output the iterate with the smallest certificate, and verify that iterate once. On the benchmark's biased Leduc family a pool of sixteen training-free solvers, seven original and nine recent variants, solves $89\%$ of the $64$ instances at threshold $10^{-5}$ this way, matching the trajectory-minimum union of the solvers. The same protocol solves $92\%$ of the $64$ pre-registered held-out instances and $89\%$ again on a third set of $64$ instances that no earlier stage used. The zero-best-response certificate certifies all $57$ in-sample solves and all $57$ fresh ones, and $58$ of the $59$ held-out ones. Its exact-comparator refinement certifies every solve in the three sets. The certificate states both and attributes its bound. Code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/CertNE.
item.dc:creator: Boning Li, Longbo Huang

item.title: GSP Autobidding Equilibria with Few Advertisers or Slots
item.description: arXiv:2610.29310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In sponsored-shopping auctions, one advertiser may win several positions, and a product that is never displayed may determine the prices of several winners. Under generalized second-price (GSP) pricing without self-pricing, these interactions couple allocation and payment through a single global ranking. We prove that exact autobidding equilibria under budget and return-on-investment (ROI) constraints can be computed in polynomial time whenever either the number $n$ of advertisers or the number $K$ of display slots is fixed. Our algorithms rely on two structural reductions. With few advertisers, the payment polytopes of tied bid layers combine by a Minkowski sum, giving a fixed-dimensional representation of exponentially many rankings. With few slots, budget equilibria admit threshold recovery and an exact submodular description of attainable payments at the display boundary. For ROI, we prove that every group-consecutive equilibrium has a representative with at most $K+2$ nonunit multipliers, preserving the item and price in every displayed slot. In each case, the reduction leads to polynomially many systems of polynomial equations and inequalities in bounded dimension. The algorithms compute exact multipliers and explicit distributions over valid group-consecutive rankings, with support at most $n+1$; for ROI with few slots, this improves to $\min\{n+1,K+3\}$.
item.dc:creator: Yiyang Huang, Zhengyang Liu, Yonglei Yan, Zihe Wang

item.title: Formalizing Cooperation and Competition: An AI-Assisted Mathematical Addendum to a 2018 Planning Thesis
item.description: arXiv:2610.29637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an AI-assisted mathematical addendum to Strategic Trip Planning: Striking a Balance Between Competition and Cooperation (Amar, 2018). We reconstruct selected relationships between strategic choice, cooperative stability, participant approval and enforcement. The thesis's Nash-to-core proposition is under-specified until outsider opportunities are stated. We verify two-person implications under fixed outsiders and explicit efficiency conditions. Under isolation, the original example has an empty TU core; its funded counterpart uses an explicit external subsidy. For a monotone resource model we characterize the exact financing gap. A finite negotiation procedure implemented in Lean is proved to terminate with participant approval, joint-cost non-worsening and local optimality against permitted approved moves. Supporting formalizations address bargaining geometry and regret-based efficiency. A resource-game counterinstance shows why monotonicity alone provides no uniform price-of-anarchy bound. Reproducible computations compare a documented heuristic reconstruction with the verified procedure on 44 source-based instances and 96 starting cases from four additional synthetic network families. Acceptance-matched heuristic and randomized pairwise-search controls contextualize the optimization results. The mathematical ingredients are established results; the contribution is a traceable reconstruction linking source statements, explicit assumptions, checked proofs, executable code and retained counterinstances. The study illustrates how AI-assisted investigation can turn engineering intuitions from legacy research into precise mathematical claims whose conditions and computational consequences can be inspected and reproduced.
item.dc:creator: Haitham Masaud Amar

item.title: Computing the Nucleon of Matching Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.29731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The nucleon is the multiplicative counterpart of the nucleolus: it lexicographically maximizes the fraction of its stand-alone value that each coalition receives. We study exact nucleon computation in matching games and in two extensions: $b$-matching games, in which players may have several partners, and partitioned matching games, in which one player may own several vertices. We resolve three open problems from a recent survey. For ordinary matching games with nonnegative rational weights, we give a polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm using maximum-weight matching, shortest paths, and minimum-cost flow, ; it returns both a nucleon allocation and a compact description of the full nucleon. In contrast, computing any nucleon allocation is NP-hard for unit-weight $b$-matching games with capacities at most three and for unit-weight partitioned matching games of width at most three. Finally, for the unresolved capacity-two case, we show that exact nucleon computation is polynomial-time Turing reducible to SHORTEST NON-ZERO CYCLE.
item.dc:creator: Haris Aziz, Gergely Cs\'aji

item.title: A Quasipolynomial Algorithm for $\ell_\infty$ Contractions
item.description: arXiv:2610.30122v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an algorithm for computing an $\eps$-approximate fixed point of any $d$-dimensional nonexpansion with respect to the $\ell_\infty$ norm in time $\log(1/\eps)^{O(\log^2 d)}$. At its core, our method uses a boosting argument to geometrically shrink a search region. Among other consequences, our algorithm implies that simple stochastic games can be solved in quasipolynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Ashkan Soleymani, Gabriele Farina

item.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.28787v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.
item.dc:creator: Hieu Tran, Hong Yu

item.title: Nashtopes and their A-discriminants
item.description: arXiv:2610.29889v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An $n$-player game in normal form is said to be of format $\boldsymbol{d} = (d_1, \dots, d_n)$ if the $i$-th player has $d_i$ options for $1 \le i \le n$, and is said to be balanced if $d_n - 1 \le \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(d_i - 1)$. The Nash equilibria of the game correspond to solutions of the system of indifference equations for the game, with payoff differences as coefficients and strategy probabilities as variables. As such, the mixed discriminant of this system gives some information about which games could have an unusual number of totally mixed Nash equilibria. This mixed discriminant can be regarded as an $\mathcal{A}$-discriminant for some matrix $\mathcal{A}$ in the sense of [Gelfand--Kapranov--Zelevinsky 1994], and the convex hull of the columns of $\mathcal{A}$ is a polytope, which we call the Nashtope. We study this $\mathcal{A}$-discriminant for each balanced game format with at least three players. This discriminant is a subset of the Nash discriminant variety introduced in [Abo--Portakal--Sodomaco 2026]. We compute the codimension and degree of this discriminant for all balanced game formats, including on-boundary formats, using the Euler obstruction formula in [Matsui--Takeuchi 2011]. Our $\mathcal{A}$-discriminant locus corresponds to a special multigraded Hurwitz locus studied in [Pratt--Sodomaco--Sturmfels 2026]. As a consequence of [Pokidkin 2026], we obtain the codimensions and degrees of the irreducible components of the Nash discriminant variety for each balanced game format with at least three players, fully resolving Problem 3.8 of [Abo--Portakal--Sodomaco 2026].
item.dc:creator: Elke Neuhaus, Irem Portakal, Luca Sodomaco, Katherine Tung

item.title: Allocating Indivisible Goods to Strategic Agents: Pure Nash Equilibria and Fairness
item.description: arXiv:2109.08644v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the problem of fairly allocating a set of indivisible goods to a set of strategic agents with additive valuation functions. We assume no monetary transfers and, therefore, a mechanism in our setting is an algorithm that takes as input the reported -- rather than the true -- values of the agents. Our main goal is to explore whether there exist mechanisms that have pure Nash equilibria for every instance and, at the same time, provide fairness guarantees for the allocations that correspond to these equilibria. We focus on two relaxations of envy-freeness, namely envy-freeness up to one good (EF1), and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), and we positively answer the above question. In particular, we study two algorithms that are known to produce such allocations in the non-strategic setting: Round-Robin (EF1 allocations for any number of agents) and a cut-and-choose algorithm of Plaut and Roughgarden [SIAM Journal of Discrete Mathematics, 2020] (EFX allocations for two agents). For Round-Robin we show that all of its pure Nash equilibria induce allocations that are EF1 with respect to the underlying true values, while for the algorithm of Plaut and Roughgarden we show that the corresponding allocations not only are EFX but also satisfy maximin share fairness, something that is not true for this algorithm in the non-strategic setting! Further, we show that a weaker version of the latter result holds for any mechanism for two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria which all induce EFX allocations.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Amanatidis, Georgios Birmpas, Federico Fusco, Philip Lazos, Stefano Leonardi, Rebecca Reiffenh\"auser

item.title: Connecting Strategy Improvement, the Simplex Algorithm and Lopsidedness
item.description: arXiv:2509.16075v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The strategy improvement algorithm for mean payoff games and parity games is a local improvement algorithm, just like the simplex algorithm for linear programs. Their similarity has turned out very useful: many lower bounds on running time for the simplex algorithm have been created, by first constructing lower bounds for strategy improvement in a game, and then transforming these into a linear program. However, earlier connections between these algorithms required constructing an intermediate Markov decision process, which is not always possible. We prove a formal, direct connection between the two algorithms, showing that many variants of strategy improvement for parity and mean payoff games are truly an instance of the simplex algorithm, under mild nondegeneracy assumptions. The linear programming formulation of these games leads to what we call hypercubelike polyhedra. These polyhedra allow us to show combinatorial properties of various games on graphs. In particular, we show a connection between strategy sets of games and lopsided sets.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Maat

item.title: Deterministic algorithms for inhomogeneous Bernoulli trials: Shapley value of network devices
item.description: arXiv:2510.07572v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Suppose that $n$ computer devices are to be connected to a network via inhomogeneous Bernoulli trials. The Shapley value of a device quantifies how much the network's value increases due to the participation of that device. Characteristic functions of such games are naturally taken as the belief function (containment function) and Choquet capacity (hitting probability) of a random set (random network of devices). Traditionally, the Shapley value is either calculated as the expected marginal contribution over all possible coalitions (subnetworks), which results in exponential computational complexity, or approximated by the Monte Carlo sampling technique, where the performance is highly dependent on the stochastic sampling process. The purpose of this study is to design deterministic algorithms for games formulated via inhomogeneous Bernoulli trials that approximate the Shapley value in linear or quadratic time, with rigorous error analysis (Sections 3 and 4). Additionally, we provide a review of relevant literature on existing calculation methods in Remark 3.1 and Appendix I. A further goal is to supplement Shapley's original proof by deriving the Shapley value formula using a rigorous approach based on definite integrals and combinatorial analysis. This method explicitly highlights the roles of the Binomial Theorem and the Beta function in the proof, addressing a gap in Shapley's work (Appendix II).
item.dc:creator: Jesse D Wei, Guo Wei

item.title: Blockchain Monetary Policy, Strategic Participation, and the Dynamics of Decentralization
item.description: arXiv:2512.16514v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Blockchain systems must navigate a fundamental tradeoff between rewarding capable participants for performance and preserving a sufficiently decentralized distribution of stake. We study this tradeoff through algorithmic reward policies in dynamic blockchain environments with publicly known capability types and evolving token stakes. We analyze two settings. First, under full participation, we study virtual-stake policies that combine type and stake in winner selection. We show that fixed virtual-stake rules exhibit strong path dependence, and that this limitation extends to broader winner-selection rules based on virtual stake; when the type weight varies over time, the winner distribution asymptotically approaches either stake-proportional or type-proportional selection. Second, we study a repeated participation game in which agents may abstain, rewards update stake, and token value depends on the decentralization of the participating stake. We characterize stage equilibria under myopic behavior. In this environment, strongly performance-favoring winner-take-most policies can drive the system to minimum decentralization under myopic play. We then identify policies that preserve participation or decentralization only by departing from strict performance-first reward design. In particular, our analysis identifies three benchmarks: policies that spread winner eligibility across the top-$k$ types, policies that simulate lookahead, and broad-sharing reward rules. Each mitigates failures of performance-first designs with different tradeoffs in participation, robustness, and performance priority. Overall, our results suggest that winner selection alone does not robustly resolve the capability-stake tradeoff: sustaining decentralization requires reward rules that react explicitly to concentration, even when this entails sacrificing some immediate performance advantage.
item.dc:creator: Diodato Ferraioli, Paolo Penna, Manvir Schneider, Carmine Ventre

item.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
item.description: arXiv:2610.28141v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Anagnostides, Constantinos Daskalakis, Gabriele Farina, Noah Golowich, Tuomas Sandholm, Brian Hu Zhang

item.title: Disjoint Stable Matchings in Linear Time
item.description: arXiv:2011.13248v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that given a SM instance G as input we can find a largest collection of pairwise edge-disjoint stable matchings of G in time linear in the input size. This extends two classical results: 1. The Gale-Shapley algorithm, which can find at most two ("extreme") pairwise edge-disjoint stable matchings of G in linear time, and 2. The polynomial-time algorithm for finding a largest collection of pairwise edge-disjoint perfect matchings (without the stability requirement) in a bipartite graph, obtained by combining K\"{o}nig's characterization with Tutte's f-factor algorithm. Moreover, we also give an algorithm to enumerate all maximum-length chains of disjoint stable matchings in the lattice of stable matchings of a given instance. This algorithm takes time polynomial in the input size for enumerating each chain. We also derive the expected number of such chains in a random instance of Stable Matching. For the Stable Roomates problem, we show that determining if a given instance admits at most two disjoint stable matchings or three disjoint stable matchings is NP-complete.
item.dc:creator: Aadityan Ganesh, Vishwa Prakash HV, Prajakta Nimbhorkar, Geevarghese Philip

item.title: AI-driven Prices for Externalities and Sustainability in Production Markets
item.description: arXiv:2106.06060v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Traditional competitive markets do not account for negative externalities; indirect costs that some participants impose on others, such as the cost of over-appropriating a common-pool resource (which diminishes future stock, and thus harvest, for everyone). Quantifying appropriate interventions to market prices has proven to be quite challenging. We propose a practical approach to computing market prices and allocations via a deep reinforcement learning policymaker agent, operating in an environment of other learning agents. Our policymaker allows us to tune the prices with regard to diverse objectives such as sustainability and resource wastefulness, fairness, buyers' and sellers' welfare, etc. As a highlight of our findings, our policymaker is significantly more successful in maintaining resource sustainability, compared to the market equilibrium outcome, in scarce resource environments.
item.dc:creator: Panayiotis Danassis, Aris Filos-Ratsikas, Haipeng Chen, Milind Tambe, Boi Faltings

item.title: RuleSmith: Multi-Agent LLMs for Automated Game Balancing
item.description: arXiv:2602.06232v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Game balancing is a longstanding challenge requiring repeated playtesting, expert intuition, and extensive manual tuning. We introduce RuleSmith, a framework that couples multi-agent LLM self-play with surrogate-based optimization over a parameterized rule space. As a proof of concept, we build CivMini, a simplified civilization-style game with two asymmetric factions governed by 12 tunable parameters. LLM agents interpret textual rulebooks and game states to propose actions that are validated by the game engine, yielding noisy estimates of faction win rates. Our primary implementation uses Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization with Expected-Improvement-based adaptive sampling to allocate more evaluation games to promising candidates. RuleSmith consistently finds near-balanced configurations: three independent optimization runs reach near-even empirical win rates in independent 200- and 300-game evaluations, and additional experiments with NTBEA and TPE show that the same self-play interface supports different search components. Cross-model evaluations and small human studies provide preliminary evidence of transfer across player populations. RuleSmith produces interpretable numerical rule adjustments without task-specific policy training. Project and code: https://adonis-galaxy.github.io/RuleSmith-website/
item.dc:creator: Ziyao Zeng, Hao Wang, Chen Liu, Youheng Yao, Jingcheng Ni, Tianyu Liu, Xiatao Sun, Fengyu Yang, Chenyu You, Xiaofeng Liu, Daniel Rakita, Ronald R. Coifman, Yuval Kluger, Zhiwen Fan

item.title: Learning to Allocate Resources with Censored Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2602.06565v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study an online resource allocation problem in which at each round, a budget $B$ must be allocated across $K$ arms under censored feedback. An arm yields a reward if and only if two conditions are satisfied: (i) the arm is activated according to an arm-specific Bernoulli random variable with unknown parameter, and (ii) the allocated budget exceeds a random threshold drawn from a parametric distribution with unknown parameter. Over $T$ rounds, the learner must jointly estimate the unknown parameters and allocate the budget so as to maximize cumulative reward facing the exploration--exploitation trade-off. We prove a worst-case regret lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ for the general model, even with known uniform threshold distributions. We then propose RA-UCB, an optimistic algorithm that leverages non-trivial parameter estimation and confidence bounds. When the budget $B$ is known at the beginning of each round, RA-UCB achieves a regret bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$, and even $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}\text{-}\log T)$ under stronger assumptions. As for unknown, round dependent budget, we introduce \texttt{MG-UCB}, which allows within-round switching and infinitesimal allocations, and matches the regret guarantees of RA-UCB. We then validate our theoretical results through experiments on real-world datasets.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Montanari, C\^ome Fiegel, Corentin Pla, Aadirupa Saha, Vianney Perchet

item.title: Moment Ambiguity and the Limits of Robust Stochastic Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2609.31090v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study fundamental information-theoretic limits of robust stochastic optimization when the distribution is known only through its exact moment sequence. We develop a unified framework that produces families of distinct distributions sharing all moments yet inducing radically different optimal decisions, thereby establishing strong impossibility results for a range of decision problems under moment ambiguity. Our binary and $N$-way moment-matching constructions separate quantiles, threshold regions, and online selection opportunities while preserving every moment. For the newsvendor problem, moment equivalence causes quantile ambiguity, inducing any fixed or randomized order quantity to fail arbitrarily badly. For revenue maximization, no deterministic or randomized posted pricing scheme can secure a nontrivial approximation relative to the full-information benchmark. For the secretary problem with cardinal observations, the optimal robust success probability under exact moment disclosure is the classical finite-horizon value $s_m$, even for i.i.d. observations. This value converges to $1/e$, compared with the full-information limit of approximately $0.5801$ due to Gilbert and Mosteller (J. Am. Stat. Assoc., 1966). We also recover and expand upon the recent impossibility result of Correa et al. (STOC, 2026) for prophet inequalities with moment knowledge. For every fixed $r\ge1$, exact moment knowledge can yield at best a $\Theta(1/\log m)$ competitive ratio, even when competing against relaxed benchmarks based on expected $r$-th order statistics or when the algorithm is allowed to select $r$ items.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'es Cristi, Matteo Russo, Jiechen Zhang
